screens.title: Introduction to Metaclasses
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we lift the curtain on metaclasses. If classes define how instances behave, then metaclasses define how classes behave. You will learn the core idea that a class is an instance of a metaclass, that Python’s built-in type is the default metaclass, and that a custom metaclass gives you a hook into the class creation lifecycle. We will also walk through practical examples showing how to inject attributes, enforce that classes implement required methods, and where to place code: in new to change the attributes before the class exists, or in init to validate the completed class. Understanding metaclasses matters when you need centralized registries, domain-specific class behaviours, or elegant enforcement of interfaces. Along the way we’ll highlight common pitfalls such as trying to change the attrs dictionary in init, and we’ll practice building a simple metaclass that injects a placeholder method and raises a clear error if a required method is not implemented. By the end you should be comfortable reading metaclass code and deciding when a metaclass is the right tool.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Introduction to Metaclasses
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Metaclasses: classes that make classes

Learn how Python constructs class objects, when the metaclass intervenes, and how to implement simple custom metaclasses to enforce structure and inject behavior.

16:9 HD Classroom
In this lesson
Understanding type, __new__, __init__, and practical metaclass patterns.
Coming up
Code walkthrough of a custom metaclass that injects methods and logs lifecycle events.
Why it matters
Use metaclasses to centralize rules, register classes, or create DSL-style class behavior.
Concept Map
Object model snapshot
object → MyClass → my_instance and type → MyMetaclass → MyClass
This shows that classes are normal objects created by a metaclass. You can swap type with a custom metaclass to change how classes are built.
Starter code snapshot
# Example: default behaviour
class MyClass:
  pass

# Implicitly created by type
# Equivalent low-level: MyClass = type('MyClass', (), {})
Quick uses
  • Central registry of subclasses
  • Inject attributes or placeholder methods
  • Enforce naming or interface rules at definition time
Key takeaway

Metaclasses run when Python builds a class. Use __new__ to alter attributes before the class exists, and __init__ to validate the finished class.

Explore Key Topics
Default metaclass: type
type constructs classes when you use the class statement.
__new__ vs __init__
__new__ creates the class object; __init__ runs after creation for validation.
Practical pattern: Interface enforcement
Inject a placeholder method that raises NotImplementedError when missing.

Attach a metaclass
Use the metaclass keyword in a class definition so Python uses your custom factory instead of type.

screens.title: What is a metaclass?
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear definition: a metaclass is a class whose instances are themselves classes. That means when Python executes a class statement it calls a metaclass to create the class object. By default the metaclass is type, so writing a normal class is roughly equivalent to calling type with the class name, base classes, and the attribute mapping. Concretely, type receives the name, the tuple of base classes, and the attrs dictionary created from the class body. When you want to change the way classes are built — for example to add a default attribute, register the class, or check for required methods — you provide a custom metaclass that inherits from type and override its lifecycle methods. An important mental model: instances live below classes, classes live below metaclasses. A frequent misconception is thinking metaclasses affect instance construction; they don't directly. Metaclasses intervene at class creation time, not every instance creation. Example: adding METACLASS_INJECTED_VAR inside a metaclass will appear as a class attribute available to all instances. Quick check: if you can solve the problem by modifying instances or by a decorator, prefer those; use a metaclass when you need a single central hook at definition time. How will you spot when a metaclass is required? Look for needs to enforce consistent class structure across many classes or to build frameworks that rely on class-level metadata.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is a metaclass?
Definition

Classes as instances of a metaclass

A metaclass receives the class name, bases, and attrs mapping and returns a class object. Use a custom metaclass to control this creation step.

Concrete example

If a metaclass adds METACLASS_INJECTED_VAR, every class created by it will expose that attribute and instances can read it.

Misconception
Metaclasses don’t run on every instance creation; they run once when the class is built.
Why it matters
Centralizing class rules simplifies frameworks, ORMs, and consistent APIs across many classes.
Analogy

Factory metaphor

Think of a metaclass as the factory that makes blueprints. Instances are products made from blueprints. If you want to change the blueprint itself, change the factory.

Quick code reminder
# Implicit: MyClass = type('MyClass', (object,), {...})
class MyClass:
  pass
Key Takeaway

Use metaclasses when you must control or validate how many classes are defined across a codebase at definition time.

screens.title: Class creation lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the class creation lifecycle is essential to using metaclasses correctly. When Python encounters a class statement, it builds an attributes mapping from the class body, then determines which metaclass to use — defaulting to type unless the class specifies a metaclass keyword. The metaclass. new method is called first with four arguments: the metaclass itself, the name of the class to create, the tuple of base classes, and the attrs dictionary. new is responsible for creating and returning the class object, typically by calling super(). new and passing a modified attrs if required. After the class object exists, the metaclass. init method runs with the new class object and the same name, bases, and attrs. init should perform validation or setup on the finished class; it cannot change the original construction step. A common mistake is attempting to mutate attrs in init expecting the class to change; by then the class is already built. Concrete example: inject a default attribute inside new, then in init log that the class is initialized or enforce a naming convention. Misconception check: new is not instance creation for object instances; it creates the class object itself. Takeaway: choose new to alter definition, init to validate.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle
keyIdea.text: metaclass.__new__ runs first to create the class; metaclass.__init__ runs after to initialize and validate the created class.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Class creation lifecycle
Process

Steps Python follows to build a class

1
Collect attrs: Python evaluates the class body and builds the attrs dictionary containing methods and variables.
2
Select metaclass: Use metaclass keyword or default to type.
3
Call __new__: metaclass.__new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs) creates and returns the class object.
4
Call __init__: metaclass.__init__(cls, name, bases, attrs) initializes and can validate the created class.
Example
# In __new__ you can add attrs before the class exists
class MyMetaclass(type):
  def __new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs):
    attrs['METACLASS_INJECTED_VAR'] = f"Hello from {name}"
    return super().__new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs)
Misconception
Changing attrs in __init__ will not change how the class was built. __init__ runs after type.__new__ has already created the class object.
Key Takeaway

Use __new__ to inject or alter class attributes; use __init__ to validate or set up the created class object.

screens.title: __new__ in depth
screens.narratorSegment: In this walkthrough we focus on the metaclass new method. new receives four arguments: the metaclass itself, the name of the class being defined, the base classes tuple, and the attrs dictionary holding methods and class variables. The role of new is to return a class object. The usual pattern is to inspect or modify attrs first, then call super(). new to let the parent metaclass — typically type — produce the class. You can also call super(). new early, capture the returned class object, and then set attributes directly on that class before returning it. Concrete example: add a METACLASS_INJECTED_VAR, and if a required method is missing inject a placeholder that raises NotImplementedError. Here is a readable code example you can run to see print statements during class creation. Common mistake: returning something other than a class object will break the class statement. Also be careful to preserve bases if you alter them. Try to keep new deterministic and side-effect conscious because it runs at import or class definition time, not at runtime per instance. Takeaway: new is your insertion point for structural changes to the class.

keyIdea.text: __new__ creates and returns the class object; modify attrs here if you need to change the class definition.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › __new__ in depth
Pattern
Inspect attrs, add defaults or placeholders, then call super().__new__ to create the class. Optionally modify the returned class object before returning.
class MyMetaclass(type):
  def __new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs):
    print(f"__new__ called for {name}")
    # Inject a class attribute
    attrs['METACLASS_INJECTED_VAR'] = f"Hello from {name}"

    # Ensure required_method exists
    if 'required_method' not in attrs:
      def _placeholder(self):
        raise NotImplementedError(f"'{name}' must implement 'required_method'")
      attrs['required_method'] = _placeholder

    cls = super().__new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs)
    # Optionally modify cls directly
    cls._injected_after = True
    return cls
Explanation cards
Inject attributes
Add defaults into attrs so the created class includes them as real class attributes.
Placeholder methods
If a method is required but missing, add one that raises NotImplementedError to prompt implementers.
Preserve bases
Modifying bases is possible but changes the MRO; avoid unless you need to alter inheritance.
Check your understanding

What will happen if __new__ returns an object that is not a class? Try to imagine Python will raise an error at class definition time.

screens.title: __init__ in depth
screens.narratorSegment: Now let’s examine metaclass init. This method receives the fully constructed class object as the first argument, along with the name, bases, and the original attrs mapping. Because init runs after the class exists, you should use it for validation, registration, or logging rather than trying to change the definition. For example, use init to check naming conventions, register the class in a central registry, or assert that class attributes meet certain constraints. If you need to add or modify attributes so they appear on the class, do so by assigning directly to the class object returned by type. new inside new or by setting attributes on cls inside init — but remember that changes to the local attrs dictionary in init do not alter the underlying class. A common trap is attempting to influence inheritance or the methods available to instances by editing attrs in init; it will not affect the already-created class unless you assign directly to cls. Example: in init you can print class. dict. keys() to observe what attributes exist after creation and raise an informative error if a required attribute is missing. Takeaway: init is for checking, registering, and final adjustments that operate on the class object itself.

keyIdea.title: __init__ role
keyIdea.text: __init__ runs after the class exists; use it for validation, registration, or logging—not for changing the initial attrs mapping.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › __init__ in depth
Pattern
Use __init__ to validate or register the class after it has been constructed. Avoid depending on changing attrs here.
class MyMetaclass(type):
  def __init__(cls, name, bases, attrs):
    print(f"__init__ called for {name}")
    # Validate the class
    if not name.startswith('Base'):
      print(f"INFO: Non-Base class '{name}' initialized.")
    super().__init__(name, bases, attrs)
Cards
Registration
Add cls to a central registry to discover subclasses at runtime.
Validation
Check naming or attribute constraints and raise errors early to guide implementers.
Pitfall
Editing attrs here does not retroactively change the class definition. If you need to add methods, attach them directly to cls.
Key Takeaway

Use __init__ for checks and registration. If you must add behaviour, set attributes on the class object itself.

screens.title: A practical metaclass: MyMetaclass
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through the example metaclass provided in the chapter. MyMetaclass inherits from type and overrides new to print lifecycle information, inspect bases and attrs, inject a METACLASS_INJECTED_VAR, and add a placeholder required_method when missing. After calling super(). new to create the class, init prints the class attributes and performs an informational check. The example demonstrates several useful patterns: logging during class creation for debugging, injecting a default attribute that instances can access, and enforcing that classes provide a particular method by adding a placeholder that raises NotImplementedError. It also demonstrates how these print statements appear before the classes are used, highlighting that metaclass code runs at definition time. When you instantiate MyCustomClass you will see the injected attribute appears on instances and required_method exists because the metaclass added it at class creation. For AnotherClass that deliberately omits the required method, the injected placeholder raises a clear error at instance-time if called, nudging the developer to implement the method. keyIdea.title: Example purpose
keyIdea.text: Use MyMetaclass to log creation, inject attributes, and enforce the presence of methods by adding placeholders in __new__.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › MyMetaclass example
Full example
class MyMetaclass(type):
    def __new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs):
        print(f"--- Metaclass __new__ called for class {name} ---")
        print(f"  Bases: {bases}")
        print(f"  Attributes before modification: {list(attrs.keys())}")

        attrs['METACLASS_INJECTED_VAR'] = f"Hello from {name}"

        if 'required_method' not in attrs:
            print(f"  WARNING: Class {name} is missing 'required_method'. Adding a placeholder.")
            def _placeholder_method(self):
                raise NotImplementedError(f"'{name}' must implement 'required_method'")
            attrs['required_method'] = _placeholder_method

        cls = super().__new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs)
        print(f"  Class object '{name}' created by __new__.")
        return cls

    def __init__(cls, name, bases, attrs):
        print(f"--- Metaclass __init__ called for class {name} ---")
        print(f"  Class attributes after creation: {list(cls.__dict__.keys())}")
        if not name.startswith('Base'):
            print(f"  INFO: Non-Base class '{name}' initialized.")
        super().__init__(name, bases, attrs)
Notes & behavior
  • Prints at import time: You will see the metaclass prints when Python defines the class, not when you instantiate it.
  • Injected attributes: METACLASS_INJECTED_VAR appears on the class and on instances as a normal attribute lookup.
  • Placeholder methods: The placeholder raises NotImplementedError to force implementers to provide a real method.
Key Takeaway

The example demonstrates how __new__ and __init__ can be combined to both alter and validate classes during creation.

screens.title: Metaclasses vs decorators & factories
screens.narratorSegment: Metaclasses are powerful, but they are not always the best tool. Consider three options you might reach for when modifying class behavior: metaclasses, class decorators, and factory functions. Use metaclasses when you need a single, centralized hook at class definition time that applies across many classes or when building frameworks that must control many classes uniformly. Class decorators are easier to reason about and suitable when you need to transform a specific class at definition time without touching Python’s class creation mechanics. Factory functions are appropriate when you want to produce customized class objects programmatically or when creation requires parameters from runtime. Concrete example: to add a simple attribute to one class, use a decorator. To ensure every subclass in a package registers itself and adheres to interface rules, a metaclass is the right choice. Misconception: because decorators run at class creation time they are not always interchangeable with metaclasses; decorators alter the final class object but cannot intercept the low-level creation in the same way metaclasses can, such as changing base classes or the attrs mapping before type constructs the class. Final question to reflect on: does your change need to apply across many classes and intervene before the class exists? If yes, consider a metaclass.

keyIdea.text: Use metaclasses for centralized, cross-cutting changes at definition time; prefer decorators or factories for local, simpler transformations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Metaclasses vs alternatives
Metaclasses
Central hook at class creation, alter attrs and bases, register classes, enforce interfaces across many classes.
Decorators
Transform a final class object, simpler, more local, and easier to reason about for single-class changes.
Factories
Produce classes programmatically at runtime or when construction needs parameters; flexible but explicit.
Guiding question
Do you need to modify the attrs mapping or bases before the class exists, or do you just want to tweak the final class object? Modify before creation: metaclass. Tweak after creation: decorator or direct assignment.

screens.title: Assigning a metaclass
screens.narratorSegment: Assigning a metaclass to a class is straightforward: include metaclass=YourMeta in the class header. This tells Python to use YourMeta instead of the default type when constructing the class object. Pattern

metaclass keyword

Declare the metaclass on the class header or define it on a base class that others inherit from.

class MyCustomClass(metaclass=MyMetaclass):
  version = 1.0

# Or set metaclass on a base class
class Base(metaclass=MyMetaclass):
  pass

class Child(Base):
  pass  # inherits the metaclass behavior
Conflict warning
If two base classes specify incompatible metaclasses, Python raises a TypeError at class creation time.
Key Takeaway

Prefer placing metaclasses on base classes when many subclasses should share behavior; avoid repeating metaclass= everywhere.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Implement InterfaceEnforcer.__new__ to inject a placeholder process_data when missing, then test with two classes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › InterfaceEnforcer activity
Starter code
class InterfaceEnforcer(type):
    def __new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs):
        required = 'process_data'
        if required not in attrs:
            print(f"Warning: Class '{name}' is missing '{required}'. Injecting placeholder.")
            def _placeholder_process_data(self):
                raise NotImplementedError(
                    f"Class '{self.__class__.__name__}' must implement the '{required}' method."
                )
            attrs[required] = _placeholder_process_data
        return super().__new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs)

class DataProcessor(metaclass=InterfaceEnforcer):
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
    def process_data(self):
        return f"Processing: {self.data.upper()}"

class MissingProcessor(metaclass=InterfaceEnforcer):
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
Test scenario
Instantiate both processors and call process_data. Expect DataProcessor to succeed and MissingProcessor to raise NotImplementedError.
Key Takeaway

Attributes injected in __new__ are part of the final class. Use this to enforce presence of API methods at definition time.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Metaclasses can introduce surprising behavior if used without clear rules. Start by preferring simpler alternatives: use class decorators or factories if they do the job. When you must use metaclasses, document the contract clearly and keep new deterministic with minimal side effects. Avoid mutating global state indiscriminately inside metaclass methods because these changes run at import time and affect module load behavior. Be careful about metaclass conflicts: if base classes have different metaclasses, Python will attempt to compute a common compatible metaclass and may raise a TypeError. Another pitfall is assuming attrs in init will change the class; it won’t. If you add attributes in init, do so by assigning to cls. For testing, run simple import-time checks in a REPL and keep print logging minimal or gated behind a debug flag. Concrete practice: collect registration and validation in init but perform structural changes inside new. Misconception check: metaclasses are not a replacement for instance-level patterns — they’re a tool for class-level control. Final reflection: use metaclasses sparingly and prefer explicit, discoverable patterns for teams that may find metaclass magic opaque.

keyIdea.text: Prefer simpler alternatives, keep metaclass code deterministic, avoid import-time side effects, and document metaclass contracts.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Pitfalls & best practices

Pitfalls to avoid

  • Import-time side effects: heavy work in __new__ runs at import/definition time and can slow startup.
  • attrs confusion: changing attrs in __init__ does not affect the class that was already created.
  • Metaclass conflicts: incompatible metaclasses on different bases lead to TypeError.
Testing tip
Run class definitions in a REPL to observe printed lifecycle messages and validate behavior before importing into larger codebases.
Documentation
Document metaclass intent and the required attributes and methods it enforces so maintainers can easily understand the contract.
Key Takeaway

Keep metaclass code minimal, predictable, and well-documented. Use them only when central, cross-class control is required.

screens.title: Common metaclass use cases
screens.narratorSegment: Metaclasses appear in several recurring patterns. One is a registry: the metaclass adds the class to a central mapping during init, allowing frameworks to discover implementations automatically. Another pattern is implementing singletons at the class creation level: by customizing call on the metaclass you can control instance construction for all classes that use that metaclass. Domain-specific languages and ORMs often use metaclasses to build class-level metadata automatically, such as mapping class attributes to database columns. The chapter’s example focuses on attribute injection and interface enforcement, but the same hooks support these larger patterns. A key point is that these patterns centralize behavior: you change the metaclass and every class that uses it picks up the change. Misconception: metaclasses are only for magical frameworks — they’re a general tool, but because they operate globally you should prefer explicit patterns when team clarity is a priority. Example scenario: an ORM metaclass inspects attributes during new, builds a column mapping, and registers the class with the ORM registry so queries can reference it. Reflection: when designing a framework, list the cross-cutting concerns you need at definition time; if several concerns require consistent enforcement, a metaclass can be the clean central place to implement them.

Patterns
Registry
Add classes to a central registry in __init__ for discovery by frameworks.
Singleton
Control instance creation by overriding __call__ in the metaclass to return the same instance.
ORM / DSL
Build mappings or class metadata automatically by inspecting attrs in __new__.
Concrete scenario
An ORM metaclass inspects attribute types during class creation, builds a fields mapping, and registers the model class. This keeps model definitions concise while centralizing the heavy lifting in one place.
Key Takeaway

Choose metaclasses for cross-cutting, definition-time behaviour such as registries, singletons, or automatic metadata generation.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s summarize the essential ideas you should retain. First, a metaclass is a class that creates classes; classes are instances of their metaclass. Second, Python’s built-in type is the default metaclass for user-defined classes, and you can override it using the metaclass keyword argument or by inheriting from a base class that specifies a metaclass. Finally, practice caution: metaclasses run at import/definition time, can create subtle import-time side effects, and can cause metaclass conflicts if bases specify incompatible metaclasses. Keep metaclass logic minimal and well-documented so your team can maintain it.

A class that defines how other classes are created.
type

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we lift the curtain on metaclasses. If classes define how instances behave, then metaclasses define how classes behave. You will learn the core idea that a class is an instance of a metaclass, that Python’s built-in type is the default metaclass, and that a custom metaclass gives you a hook into the class creation lifecycle. We will also walk through practical examples showing how to inject attributes, enforce that classes implement required methods, and where to place code: in new to change the attributes before the class exists, or in init to validate the completed class. Understanding metaclasses matters when you need centralized registries, domain-specific class behaviours, or elegant enforcement of interfaces. Along the way we’ll highlight common pitfalls such as trying to change the attrs dictionary in init, and we’ll practice building a simple metaclass that injects a placeholder method and raises a clear error if a required method is not implemented. By the end you should be comfortable reading metaclass code and deciding when a metaclass is the right tool.

In this module you will build a practical understanding of metaclasses and how they fit into Python’s object model. First, you will be able to define what a metaclass is and explain the relationship between classes and metaclasses, using type as the canonical example. You’ll then identify where the default metaclass called type is used and why a custom metaclass might be needed. Next, you will describe the lifecycle of class creation, the order in which Python calls metaclass methods, and the distinction between new and init for metaclasses. Finally, you will implement a basic custom metaclass that overrides new to modify attributes and init to validate the created class. Each objective includes a short practical mnemonic or visual idea to help you remember the role of each method and why metaclasses are powerful but should be used judiciously.

This second objectives page focuses on practical checks and why each objective matters in real code. You will practice attaching a metaclass with the metaclass keyword argument in a class definition and see how this replaces the default type. You will also learn to implement a metaclass that injects attributes or methods at definition time, such as adding a default identifier or a placeholder method that raises NotImplementedError. Another objective is to spot a common mistake: modifying the attrs mapping in init expecting the class definition to change. We will explain why that does not work and show the correct place to mutate or inject attributes. Finally, you will be prepared to choose when to use metaclasses versus simpler alternatives like class decorators or factory functions, because metaclasses are powerful but can add cognitive load if overused.

Start with a clear definition: a metaclass is a class whose instances are themselves classes. That means when Python executes a class statement it calls a metaclass to create the class object. By default the metaclass is type, so writing a normal class is roughly equivalent to calling type with the class name, base classes, and the attribute mapping. Concretely, type receives the name, the tuple of base classes, and the attrs dictionary created from the class body. When you want to change the way classes are built — for example to add a default attribute, register the class, or check for required methods — you provide a custom metaclass that inherits from type and override its lifecycle methods. An important mental model: instances live below classes, classes live below metaclasses. A frequent misconception is thinking metaclasses affect instance construction; they don't directly. Metaclasses intervene at class creation time, not every instance creation. Example: adding METACLASS_INJECTED_VAR inside a metaclass will appear as a class attribute available to all instances. Quick check: if you can solve the problem by modifying instances or by a decorator, prefer those; use a metaclass when you need a single central hook at definition time. How will you spot when a metaclass is required? Look for needs to enforce consistent class structure across many classes or to build frameworks that rely on class-level metadata.

Understanding the class creation lifecycle is essential to using metaclasses correctly. When Python encounters a class statement, it builds an attributes mapping from the class body, then determines which metaclass to use — defaulting to type unless the class specifies a metaclass keyword. The metaclass. new method is called first with four arguments: the metaclass itself, the name of the class to create, the tuple of base classes, and the attrs dictionary. new is responsible for creating and returning the class object, typically by calling super(). new and passing a modified attrs if required. After the class object exists, the metaclass. init method runs with the new class object and the same name, bases, and attrs. init should perform validation or setup on the finished class; it cannot change the original construction step. A common mistake is attempting to mutate attrs in init expecting the class to change; by then the class is already built. Concrete example: inject a default attribute inside new, then in init log that the class is initialized or enforce a naming convention. Misconception check: new is not instance creation for object instances; it creates the class object itself. Takeaway: choose new to alter definition, init to validate.

In this walkthrough we focus on the metaclass new method. new receives four arguments: the metaclass itself, the name of the class being defined, the base classes tuple, and the attrs dictionary holding methods and class variables. The role of new is to return a class object. The usual pattern is to inspect or modify attrs first, then call super(). new to let the parent metaclass — typically type — produce the class. You can also call super(). new early, capture the returned class object, and then set attributes directly on that class before returning it. Concrete example: add a METACLASS_INJECTED_VAR, and if a required method is missing inject a placeholder that raises NotImplementedError. Here is a readable code example you can run to see print statements during class creation. Common mistake: returning something other than a class object will break the class statement. Also be careful to preserve bases if you alter them. Try to keep new deterministic and side-effect conscious because it runs at import or class definition time, not at runtime per instance. Takeaway: new is your insertion point for structural changes to the class.

Now let’s examine metaclass init. This method receives the fully constructed class object as the first argument, along with the name, bases, and the original attrs mapping. Because init runs after the class exists, you should use it for validation, registration, or logging rather than trying to change the definition. For example, use init to check naming conventions, register the class in a central registry, or assert that class attributes meet certain constraints. Let’s summarize the essential ideas you should retain. First, a metaclass is a class that creates classes; classes are instances of their metaclass. Second, Python’s built-in type is the default metaclass for user-defined classes, and you can override it using the metaclass keyword argument or by inheriting from a base class that specifies a metaclass. Third, the class creation lifecycle calls metaclass. new first — use that to change attrs or create the class — and then metaclass. init to validate or register the created class. Fourth, prefer simpler alternatives like class decorators or factory functions unless you must intervene centrally at definition time. Finally, practice caution: metaclasses run at import/definition time, can create subtle import-time side effects, and can cause metaclass conflicts if bases specify incompatible metaclasses. Keep metaclass logic minimal and well-documented so your team can maintain it.

Finish with three compact reminders you can keep in mind as you work with metaclasses. First, always decide whether a metaclass is necessary: prefer decorators or factories for simple, local tasks. Second, remember the lifecycle: new runs to create the class and is where you alter attrs for the class definition; init runs after creation for checks, registration, or logging. Third, document and test metaclass behavior because it runs at import time and affects all classes that use it.
